cloze.text: The ASA classification is a {{c1::medical risk}} scale used to predict the risk of complications during {{c2::surgery and anesthesia}}.
cloze.extra: Board Alert: in dentistry we adapt the ASA system to estimate medical risk during dental care, but it doesn't always fit perfectly.

cloze.text: {{c1::ASA I}} = {{c2::normal healthy patient}} — e.g., non-smoker, minimal alcohol use, no systemic disease.
cloze.extra: Exam standard: ASA Physical Status Classification (amended 2020).

cloze.text: {{c1::ASA II}} = {{c2::mild}} systemic disease {{c3::without}} functional limitations.
Examples of ASA {{c1::II}}: controlled hypertension or diabetes, healthy pregnancy, allergies, BMI 30–40, social alcohol use, smoking.
{{c1::ASA III}} = {{c2::severe}} systemic disease {{c3::with}} functional limitations.
Examples of ASA {{c1::III}}: poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, COPD, stable angina, history (>3 months) of MI or stroke, dialysis patient, implanted pacemaker, BMI ≥ 40.
{{c1::ASA IV}} = severe systemic disease that is a {{c2::constant threat to life}}.
Examples of ASA {{c1::IV}}: recent (<3 months) MI, stroke, or unstable angina; symptomatic CHF or COPD; hepatorenal failure.
{{c1::ASA V}} = {{c2::moribund}} patient not expected to survive without surgery — e.g., end-stage disease (ruptured aneurysm, massive trauma, terminal cancer).
{{c1::ASA VI}} = declared {{c2::brain-dead}} patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes (organ donor patient only).
When a patient has several conditions, use the {{c1::highest-risk}} condition to determine the ASA class — e.g., well-controlled asthma (ASA II) + recent MI (ASA IV) = ASA {{c2::IV}}.
{{c1::Multiple mild conditions}} may bump a patient from ASA II to ASA {{c2::III}} — e.g., controlled diabetes + controlled hypertension + smoker.
Mental health conditions such as anxiety or depression do {{c1::not}} directly change the ASA classification.
cloze.extra: Board Alert: the ASA system doesn't always fit dentistry perfectly.

cloze.text: AHA 2017 BP category {{c1::Normal}}: systolic less than {{c2::120}} AND diastolic less than {{c3::80}} mmHg.
AHA 2017 BP category {{c1::Elevated}}: systolic {{c2::120–129}} AND diastolic less than 80 mmHg.
AHA 2017 {{c1::Stage 1}} hypertension: systolic {{c2::130–139}} OR diastolic {{c3::80–89}} mmHg.
AHA 2017 {{c1::Stage 2}} hypertension: systolic {{c2::140 or higher}} OR diastolic {{c3::90 or higher}} mmHg.
AHA 2017 {{c1::Hypertensive crisis}}: systolic higher than {{c2::180}} and/or diastolic higher than {{c3::120}} mmHg — consult a doctor immediately.
Hypertension is called the "{{c1::silent killer}}" because high pressure damages vessel walls and vital organs even {{c2::without symptoms}}.
cloze.extra: Hypertension = pressure inside the blood vessels is too high over time.

cloze.text: Cause of hypertension: changes that increase {{c1::resistance}} in the vessels (normally vessels are elastic, have a smooth lining and expand with each heartbeat).
Contributors to hypertension: lifestyle and systemic factors like {{c1::smoking}}, stress, {{c2::obesity}}, diabetes, and high {{c3::salt}} intake.
BP diagnosis: the {{c1::systolic}} (top) number is the pressure when the heart {{c2::pumps}}; the {{c3::diastolic}} (bottom) number is the pressure when the heart {{c4::relaxes}}.
If systolic and diastolic fall in different BP categories, always use the {{c1::higher}} category to determine severity.
cloze.extra: e.g., 125/92 → Stage 2 (because of the diastolic).

cloze.text: Hypertension usually has {{c1::no symptoms}}, but can lead to stroke, heart attack, {{c2::kidney failure}}, or {{c3::eye}} damage.
Hypertension treatment starts with {{c1::lifestyle changes}} — less salt, more exercise, healthy weight.
Always check BP before dental care because readings ≥ {{c1::180/110}} mmHg increase the risk of stroke or heart attack.
Raise the dental chair slowly to prevent dizziness from {{c1::postural (orthostatic) hypotension}} caused by antihypertensive medications.
{{c1::Hydrochlorothiazide}} (a diuretic) and {{c2::atenolol}} (a beta-blocker) commonly cause dry mouth and low blood pressure when standing.
In hypertensive patients use caution with {{c1::epinephrine}} and avoid {{c2::sodium}}-containing air polishers — both can raise BP.
Stress-reduction protocol for hypertensive patients: {{c1::short morning}} appointments, good anesthesia, and a calm environment.
Dental BP table: BP <140/<90 → ASA {{c1::I}} → {{c2::proceed with routine care}} (healthy or well-controlled).
cloze.extra: Book's dental-management table. Note: by AHA 2017 categories, 130–139/80–89 is already Stage 1 hypertension and ≥140/90 is Stage 2.

cloze.text: Dental BP table: BP 140–159 / 90–99 → ASA {{c1::II}} → proceed with care; {{c2::monitor BP at each visit}} (mild hypertension, minimal risk, may worsen).
cloze.extra: Book's dental-management table. Note: by AHA 2017 categories, 130–139/80–89 is already Stage 1 hypertension and ≥140/90 is Stage 2.

cloze.text: Dental BP table: BP 160–179 / 100–109 → ASA {{c1::III}} → proceed with caution, recheck BP after {{c2::5}} minutes, use stress reduction, consider {{c3::medical consultation}}.
cloze.extra: Book's dental-management table. Note: by AHA 2017 categories, 130–139/80–89 is already Stage 1 hypertension and ≥140/90 is Stage 2.

cloze.text: Dental BP table: BP ≥{{c1::180}} / ≥{{c2::110}} (even once) → ASA IV → {{c3::stop elective care}}; recheck in 5 minutes and if still elevated refer for medical evaluation before treatment.
cloze.extra: Danger zone: high risk of stroke or MI — delay elective procedures.

cloze.text: A patient with any BP plus symptoms (headache, dizziness, chest pain) is ASA {{c1::IV}}: {{c2::stop immediately}} regardless of the reading and refer to emergency care or a physician.
cloze.extra: Symptoms indicate a possible hypertensive crisis or cardiac issue.

cloze.text: If a hypertensive patient skipped their meds, ask {{c1::when they last took them}}, consider rechecking BP, and delay care if pressure is high.
cloze.extra: Skipped doses = uncontrolled pressure; ASA class varies.

cloze.text: Angina is {{c1::chest pain}} that occurs when the heart muscle doesn't get enough {{c2::oxygen}} due to reduced blood flow in the {{c3::coronary arteries}}.
cloze.extra: Coronary arteries = the vessels that supply the heart itself.

cloze.text: Cause of angina: {{c1::narrowing or blockage}} of the coronary arteries.
Angina risk factors: smoking, high blood pressure, high {{c1::cholesterol}}, diabetes, obesity, emotional {{c2::stress}}, and lack of physical activity.
Angina feels like {{c1::squeezing, tightness}} in the chest that can spread to the neck, jaw, shoulder, back, or arms, usually during {{c2::exercise}}.
Angina treatment: {{c1::rest}}, medications that improve blood flow and reduce the heart's workload, and in serious cases {{c2::stent placement or bypass surgery}}.
Angina patients: ask if the patient carries their {{c1::angina medication}} and keep it {{c2::nearby}} during treatment; schedule short, calm morning appointments.
Angina emergency: stop treatment immediately and keep the patient seated {{c1::upright or semi-reclined}} to reduce stress on the heart and support breathing.
Angina emergency: give 1 dose of nitroglycerin {{c1::under the tongue}} if systolic BP is ≥ {{c2::90}} mmHg.
cloze.extra: Nitroglycerin dilates blood vessels and reduces the heart's oxygen demand.

cloze.text: Angina emergency: call 911 if the pain is not relieved after the {{c1::first}} nitroglycerin dose — this may indicate a true {{c2::heart attack}}.
Angina/MI emergency: give chewable {{c1::aspirin}} ({{c2::160–325}} mg) if the patient is not allergic and is alert, to help prevent further clot formation.
Angina emergency: be prepared to begin {{c1::CPR}} and use the {{c2::AED}} if the patient becomes unresponsive (cardiac arrest).
Sublingual nitroglycerin works {{c1::3–5}} times faster than if swallowed because it enters the bloodstream directly through the {{c2::oral mucosa}}, bypassing the digestive system and liver.
Myocardial infarction: part of the {{c1::heart muscle}} is damaged or dies due to a sudden {{c2::blockage}} in one of the coronary arteries, stopping oxygen from reaching the tissue.
MI cause: complete or near-complete blockage of a coronary artery, usually from a {{c1::blood clot}} forming over a {{c2::ruptured plaque}}.
MI risk factors: {{c1::atherosclerosis}}, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, obesity, stress, and lack of exercise.
MI: {{c1::crushing or heavy}} chest pain that may spread to the neck, jaw, shoulder, back, or arms, often with {{c2::sweating}}, nausea, shortness of breath, or feeling faint.
cloze.extra: Compare angina: squeezing/tightness, usually during exercise, relieved by rest/nitroglycerin.

cloze.text: MI treatment: emergency care with oxygen, aspirin, nitroglycerin, {{c1::clot-busting drugs}}, and procedures such as {{c2::angioplasty}} or bypass surgery to restore blood flow.
Post-MI patients: schedule {{c1::short, low-stress morning}} appointments and monitor for {{c2::anxiety}} or chest discomfort during treatment.
{{c1::Anticoagulant}} or {{c2::antiplatelet}} drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban) increase the risk of {{c3::prolonged bleeding}} during and after dental procedures.
MI emergency protocol is the same as for angina, but {{c1::911 should be called quickly}}, especially if symptoms are more severe or the patient is not responding.
Congestive heart failure: the heart becomes too {{c1::weak or stiff}} to pump effectively, so blood backs up, causing {{c2::fluid buildup}} in the lungs, legs, and other tissues.
CHF cause: heart muscle is {{c1::damaged}} (e.g., after a heart attack) or {{c2::overworked}} for years, making it too weak to push blood forward.
The {{c1::right}} side of the heart receives blood from the body and sends it to the lungs; if it fails, blood backs up in the veins and fluid pools in the {{c2::ankles, legs, and feet}} (gravity).
The {{c1::left}} side of the heart receives blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body; if it fails, fluid backs up into the {{c2::lungs}}, causing shortness of breath and coughing.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Left = Lung; Right = Rest of the body.

cloze.text: CHF risk factors: {{c1::hypertension}}, {{c2::coronary artery disease}}, diabetes, smoking, obesity, and kidney disease.
CHF signs: shortness of breath, fatigue, {{c1::swollen ankles or legs}}, and difficulty breathing when {{c2::lying flat}}.
CHF treatment: {{c1::diuretics}}, ACE inhibitors, and beta-blockers; severe cases may need devices or surgery.
CHF patients: treat only if the condition is {{c1::stable}}; get {{c2::medical clearance}} if unsure.
Position a CHF patient {{c1::upright or semi-reclined}}; lying flat can worsen {{c2::fluid buildup in the lungs}} and make breathing harder.
In CHF patients with severe breathing difficulty, avoid {{c1::power scalers}} or {{c2::rubber dam isolation}}.
CHF patients: limit {{c1::epinephrine}} (stress on the heart) and monitor for signs of fatigue or breathing trouble.
Many CHF patients take {{c1::diuretics}}, which can cause {{c2::dry mouth}} and increased urination.

A CHF patient can develop symptoms like angina or MI (chest pain, shortness of breath, fatigue); follow the {{c1::same emergency steps}}: stop treatment, upright position, nitroglycerin, oxygen, call 911 if symptoms persist.
Arrhythmia: an abnormal heart rhythm caused by problems in the heart's {{c1::electrical signals}} — the heart may beat too fast, too slow, or irregularly.
Arrhythmia causes: disruption of electrical signaling due to aging, heart damage, {{c1::electrolyte imbalance}}, medications, or stress.
Arrhythmia contributors: heart attack, high blood pressure, valve disorders, {{c1::thyroid}} issues, {{c2::stimulant}} use (e.g., caffeine), and some drugs.
Arrhythmia signs: {{c1::fluttering in the chest}}, palpitations, fatigue, dizziness, shortness of breath, or fainting.
Arrhythmia treatment: medications ({{c1::beta-blockers}}, antiarrhythmics), a pacemaker, or an implanted defibrillator.
An {{c1::implanted defibrillator (ICD)}} is like a pacemaker but also delivers a {{c2::shock}} if the heart goes into a dangerous rhythm like {{c3::ventricular fibrillation}}.
Pacemaker/ICD with {{c1::unknown}} shielding: avoid equipment that generates {{c2::electromagnetic interference}} (e.g., older ultrasonic scalers, electrosurgery units).
If pacemaker shielding is {{c1::confirmed}}, ultrasonic scalers may be used with caution — avoid placing the cord or handpiece {{c2::directly over the device}}.
In {{c1::unstable}} arrhythmias, limit epinephrine and avoid {{c2::vasoconstrictors}} unless cleared by a physician.
Arrhythmia emergency: stop treatment, keep the patient {{c1::upright}} and calm; call 911 if symptoms worsen or the patient becomes unresponsive, and prepare for {{c2::CPR and AED}}.
In a {{c1::coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)}}, a healthy blood vessel (usually from the {{c2::leg, arm, or chest}}) is harvested to create a new path around a blocked coronary artery.
cloze.extra: Prevents angina and heart attacks. WakeUpMemory: a CABG is like building a detour road around traffic.

cloze.text: Angioplasty: a tiny {{c1::balloon}} is inserted into a clogged artery and inflated to push the plaque aside; a {{c2::stent}} (small wire mesh tube) is often placed to keep the artery open long-term.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: a stent is like propping open a collapsed tunnel to let traffic (blood) through.

cloze.text: After a stent or bypass graft, {{c1::antiplatelet}} drugs like aspirin and clopidogrel (Plavix) prevent blood clots inside it; they are usually taken for {{c2::months or even years}}.
ADHD affects {{c1::focus}}, {{c2::impulse control}}, and activity level; common in children but may continue into adulthood.
ADHD cause: believed to involve {{c1::dopamine}} and {{c2::norepinephrine}} imbalance in parts of the brain that control attention and behavior.
ADHD contributors: genetics, {{c1::premature birth}}, environmental exposures (e.g., {{c2::lead}}), and possible brain development differences.
ADHD signs: trouble focusing, sitting still, following instructions, or {{c1::waiting turns}}; may interrupt or act impulsively.
ADHD is managed with behavioral therapy and {{c1::stimulant}} medications like methylphenidate ({{c2::Ritalin}}) or amphetamine ({{c3::Adderall}}).
ADHD patients: use a calm, structured approach; appointments should be {{c1::short, predictable}}, and scheduled {{c2::early in the day}}.
ADHD patients: praise cooperation, give clear simple instructions, and use the {{c1::tell-show-do}} approach.
Stimulant ADHD meds (Ritalin, Adderall) activate the {{c1::sympathetic}} nervous system, causing {{c2::dry mouth}}, {{c3::bruxism}}, or appetite loss.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Adderall = Active but Dry" — boosts focus and energy but dries the mouth. Reduced saliva + increased jaw tension.

cloze.text: Patients with ADHD may struggle with {{c1::oral hygiene routines}} or forget steps.
Alzheimer's is caused by {{c1::amyloid plaques}} (sticky protein clumps) and {{c2::tau tangles}} that destroy nerve cells, starting in the {{c3::hippocampus}} (memory center).
Alzheimer's: gradual {{c1::memory loss}}, disorientation, poor reasoning; severe memory loss early because the {{c2::hippocampus}} is affected first.
{{c1::Alzheimer's}} is the most common dementia, usually over age {{c2::65}}.
Vascular dementia is caused by {{c1::blocked or reduced blood flow}} in parts of the brain, often from a {{c2::stroke}}.
Vascular dementia shows a {{c1::step-like decline}} in thinking and motor skills after strokes or mini-strokes; memory may be preserved early if other brain areas are damaged.
cloze.extra: Other clues: history of stroke, high blood pressure, or heart disease.

cloze.text: Lewy body dementia: {{c1::Lewy bodies}} (abnormal proteins) disrupt brain signals, especially in the {{c2::cortex and brainstem}}.
Lewy body dementia: fluctuating memory, {{c1::visual hallucinations}}, tremors, confusion; confusion worsens {{c2::at night}}.
Lewy body dementia may include {{c1::acting out dreams}}, {{c2::Parkinson}}-like stiffness, and hallucinations.
Frontotemporal dementia: nerve loss in the {{c1::frontal and temporal}} lobes, which control behavior and language.
Frontotemporal dementia: {{c1::personality and behavior}} change first (inappropriate comments, apathy, impulsiveness) while memory stays intact early.
Frontotemporal dementia is more common {{c1::under}} age 65 and may be confused with {{c2::psychiatric disorders}}.
Dementia patients may {{c1::forget to brush}}, misuse products, or avoid care due to fear/confusion.
Dementia: use simple, calm language and repeat as needed; involve a {{c1::caregiver or legal guardian}} early for medical history, {{c2::consent}}, and home care.
In later-stage dementia, {{c1::swallowing difficulties}} may increase {{c2::aspiration}} risk.
Dementia patients may show {{c1::agitation, resistance}}, or even aggression during treatment.
Parkinson's is a progressive brain disorder in which the brain stops producing enough {{c1::dopamine}}, affecting movement and coordination.
Parkinson's cause: loss of dopamine-producing cells, especially in the {{c1::substantia nigra}}.
Parkinson's signs: {{c1::tremors}}, muscle stiffness, slow movements, {{c2::shuffling gait}}, and facial stiffness ({{c3::mask-like}} expression); symptoms worsen over time.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory — dopamine's dual role: 1. Movement (too little = shaking, stiffness, slow motion); 2. Motivation & mood (too little = depression-like symptoms).

cloze.text: Parkinson's has no cure; it is managed with dopamine-replacement drugs like {{c1::levodopa}} (often combined with {{c2::carbidopa}}), or {{c3::deep brain stimulation}}.
Parkinson's patients: use {{c1::short, stress-free}} appointments to reduce fatigue and anxiety.
Parkinson's patients: use a {{c1::mouth prop}} if the patient has tremors or trouble holding the mouth open.
{{c1::Xerostomia}} is a common side effect of Parkinson's drugs (e.g., levodopa).
Parkinson's patients: protect the {{c1::airway}} to prevent choking, and stabilize the patient's {{c2::hands}} with aids to prevent injuries from the tremor.
Stroke (CVA): sudden loss of brain function due to a {{c1::blocked or burst}} blood vessel in the brain.
A {{c1::blood clot}} blocking a cerebral artery causes an {{c2::ischemic}} stroke, often due to atherosclerosis.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "I see a clot" — I C = Ischemic = Clot.

cloze.text: Bleeding from a ruptured vessel causes a {{c1::hemorrhagic}} stroke.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: if it's not a clot, it's a POP — H = Hemorrhagic = Pop (the vessel bursts and bleeds into the brain).

cloze.text: Stroke risk factors: high blood pressure, atherosclerosis, heart disease, smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, and {{c1::age}}.
Stroke signs: sudden numbness or weakness (often {{c1::one side}}), slurred speech, confusion, vision changes, or severe {{c2::headache}}.
Each half of the brain controls the {{c1::opposite}} side of the body: a stroke in the left brain causes {{c2::right}}-side weakness.
Stroke treatment: emergency {{c1::clot-busting drugs}} or surgery to restore blood flow; {{c2::rehab}} for movement or speech may follow.
Post-stroke patients: short, stress-free appointments and {{c1::monitor blood pressure}}; avoid {{c2::epinephrine}} if stroke risk or uncontrolled hypertension is present.
Stroke emergency: stop treatment, keep the patient upright and calm, call 911 and note the {{c1::exact time symptoms began}}.
Stroke emergency: give nothing {{c1::by mouth}} (no medications, water, or food); {{c2::aspirin}} would be dangerous if it is a hemorrhagic stroke (could worsen bleeding).

basic.front: What does ASA stand for (ASA physical status classification)?
Pregnancy is not a disease — so why is a healthy pregnant patient classified ASA II?

basic.back: Arteries become stiff and lose flexibility, making it harder for blood to flow
Fatty plaque builds up inside the arteries and narrows the space for blood to pass through
When a drug that is swallowed is mostly destroyed by the liver before it can take effect (e.g., oral nitroglycerin)
basic.extra: That's why nitroglycerin is given sublingually.

basic.front: Heart attack vs cardiac arrest — what's the difference?
basic.back: A heart attack is a circulation problem (blocked blood flow); cardiac arrest is an electrical problem where the heart stops beating.
A small device placed under the skin (usually near the shoulder) that sends electrical signals to keep the heart beating at a regular rate

typein.question: History of MI or stroke: more than how many months ago makes it ASA III rather than ASA IV? (number)
typein.extra: History (>3 months) of MI/stroke = ASA III; recent (<3 months) = ASA IV.

typein.question: Maximum epinephrine in local anesthetic for a patient with angina or a history of MI? (mg)
typein.extra: About two cartridges of 1:100,000 (book pp. 204, applies to angina and MI).

typein.question: Angina emergency: nitroglycerin may be repeated every how many minutes? (number)
Angina emergency: maximum total number of nitroglycerin doses? (number)
Per the book, do not treat a patient who had a heart attack within the past how many months without medical clearance? (number)
typein.extra: Book's rule. Note the ASA table (p.202) uses <3 months = recent MI = ASA IV.

typein.question: Parkinson's: schedule treatment how long after the medication dose, when it is most effective? (minutes)
After a stroke, wait how many months before dental treatment unless physician clearance is given? (number)

mcq.question: A 58-year-old patient has controlled type 2 diabetes and controlled hypertension, and smokes 20 cigarettes per day. Which ASA class is most appropriate?
mcq.explanation: Each condition alone is ASA II, but multiple mild conditions can bump the patient to ASA III (the book's own example). ASA IV would need a constant threat to life, such as a recent MI.

mcq.question: A patient with well-controlled asthma had a myocardial infarction 6 weeks ago. What is the ASA classification?
mcq.explanation: Use the highest-risk condition: a recent (<3 months) MI is ASA IV. The asthma alone would be ASA II; an MI more than 3 months ago would be ASA III.

mcq.question: A patient's blood pressure is 128/84 mmHg. According to the AHA 2017 categories, this is:
mcq.explanation: 128 alone would be Elevated, but the diastolic 84 falls in Stage 1 (80–89). When the numbers fall in different categories, use the higher one.

mcq.question: Before scaling, a patient's BP is 184/112 mmHg. Five minutes later it is 182/110 and the patient feels fine. What should the hygienist do?
options: B. Proceed, using a stress-reduction protocol
C. Stop elective care and refer for medical evaluation
mcq.answer: C. Stop elective care and refer for medical evaluation
mcq.explanation: ≥180/≥110 (even once) = ASA IV: stop elective care, recheck in 5 minutes, and refer if still elevated. A stress-reduction protocol is for the 160–179/100–109 range.

mcq.question: During scaling, a patient with a history of angina reports squeezing chest pain. Treatment is stopped and the patient is seated upright; BP is 132/84. What is the next step?
options: A. Place the patient supine with legs raised
B. Give one sublingual nitroglycerin dose
mcq.answer: B. Give one sublingual nitroglycerin dose
mcq.explanation: Systolic is ≥90 mmHg, so give one nitroglycerin dose under the tongue (repeat every 5 min, max 3); call 911 if pain is not relieved after the first dose. Lying flat is not recommended — keep the patient upright or semi-reclined.

mcq.question: Which finding best distinguishes a myocardial infarction from an angina attack in the dental chair?
options: A. Chest pain spreading to the jaw or arm
B. Chest pain not relieved by nitroglycerin
mcq.answer: B. Chest pain not relieved by nitroglycerin
mcq.explanation: Angina pain is relieved by rest and nitroglycerin; if pain is not relieved after the first dose, suspect a true heart attack and call 911. Radiating pain occurs in both.

mcq.question: A patient with congestive heart failure arrives short of breath. Which modification is most appropriate?
options: A. Supine position with ultrasonic scaling
B. Upright or semi-reclined position; avoid power scalers
C. Rubber dam for all procedures
D. Trendelenburg position to improve blood flow
mcq.answer: B. Upright or semi-reclined position; avoid power scalers
mcq.explanation: Lying flat worsens fluid in the lungs; seat the patient upright/semi-reclined and avoid power scalers and rubber dams when breathing is severely difficult.

mcq.question: A patient has a pacemaker, but its shielding status is unknown. Which instrument is the best choice for calculus removal?
options: D. Any ultrasonic, with the cord over the device
mcq.explanation: With unknown shielding, avoid equipment that generates electromagnetic interference (older ultrasonic scalers, electrosurgery). Even when shielding is confirmed, never place the cord over the device.

mcq.question: A 10-year-old taking methylphenidate (Ritalin) for ADHD is most likely to present with which oral finding?
mcq.explanation: Stimulants activate the sympathetic nervous system, reducing saliva and increasing jaw tension ("Adderall = Active but Dry").

mcq.question: A 59-year-old patient's spouse reports he has recently started making inappropriate comments and seems apathetic, though his memory seems fine. Which dementia is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia: personality/behavior change first with memory intact early, more common under 65. Alzheimer's starts with memory loss, usually over 65.

mcq.question: During treatment, a patient suddenly develops slurred speech and drooping on the right side of the face. After calling 911, which action is CONTRAINDICATED?
options: A. Noting the time symptoms began
B. Keeping the patient upright and calm
mcq.explanation: Give nothing by mouth to a suspected stroke patient: aspirin could worsen bleeding in a hemorrhagic stroke (unlike the angina/MI protocol, where aspirin helps).
